newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH CABINET TO QUIT IF TAX CUT TOO DEEP - KOLODKO.
newsitem.headline: POLISH CABINET TO QUIT IF TAX CUT TOO DEEP - KOLODKO.

text.p: Polish Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko said on Wednesday his government would rather quit than implement new lower tax levels unexpectedly passed by the lower house of parliament last month.

"If the Sejm (lower house) proposals went through the government...would resign because it would not be able to take responsibility for measures that are wrong from the economic point of view and irresponsible politically," Kolodko told a Senate committee debating the taxes.

The chances of the Sejm bill, introducing four tax rates and a new lowest 17 percent tax band, coming into force is limited, as President Aleksander Kwasniewski has signalled he would veto the bill as economically unrealistic.

After the session, Kolodko, who was trying to win Senators' support for the government's proposal of moderate tax cuts, softened his earlier statement on possible resignation, saying the government still hoped the Senate would back its tax plan.
"I cannot rule out any situation but the question (of resignation) is premature and I believe that economic thinking will prevail," Kolodko told reporters.

The Senate legislative committee postponed a decision on whether to support or reject the lower house's bill to Thursday and another upper house body, the national economy committee, was due to discuss the issue later on Wednesday.
The government proposes cutting taxes to 20, 31 and 43 percent next year from this year's 21, 33 and 45 percent.
The bigger partner in the ruling coalition, the Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) backs the government proposals.
The Polish Peasant Party (PSL), supported an opposition bill in the lower house which would introduce four levels at 17, 20, 33 and 45 -- a move designed to help low-earners.
The Peasants have signalled they might give up the four-level scale if tax cuts for the low-paid were deeper than those proposed by the government and they also seek fuel subsidies for farmers.
But the two coalition parties, who together enjoy a comfortable majority in both houses of parliament, have far failed to reach an agreement on how to vote in the Senate.

Kolodko said the government plan for limited tax reductions would require amending the 1997 budget, which assumes unchanged taxes, and widening the budget gap to 2.8 percent of gross domestic product from an earlier planned 2.6 percent.

But he said it would be possible to finance the slightly higher deficit without boosting inflation, while the lower house's proposals would create a 3.6 billion zloty gap in revenues, which would be impossible to finance.
